image.prompt:
Product photograph of one isolated object, shot from a HIGH THREE-QUARTER ANGLE: the camera is well above the object and tilted down about 30 degrees, so the top of the object is clearly visible along with its front and one side. Not a straight-on elevation.

The object: One short straight section of a galvanised steel vertical ladder, free-standing as a single detached piece: two flat-bar side stiles with round rungs between them, two short steel standoff brackets with flat bolt plates projecting from the back, cut flat at top and bottom. No wall, no building, no ground. Materials: Galvanised steel gone dull grey, red-oxide primer showing at the bolt plates, rust streaks running down from the welds, grime on the rung tops.

Form: build the object from a few simple, chunky, closed volumes. Prefer solid panels over lattice, mesh, grilles or perforated screens; keep any openings few, large and clearly separated. No thin spindly protrusions, no wires, no chains, no fringes, no lace, no fine filigree, no dense repeated slots or cut-outs. Keep the silhouette simple and readable from every side. Keep the object's SHAPE simple; richness must come from the surface finish, wear and materials rather than from intricate geometry. The object is still photoreal and highly detailed in its texture -- only its form is simple.

Framing: long-lens near-orthographic perspective, minimal foreshortening. The object is perfectly centred and occupies about 75% of the frame height, with clear empty margin on all four sides. The whole object is in frame; nothing is cropped.

Background: completely flat seamless neutral 50% grey (#808080). The object floats in empty space against an infinite seamless backdrop, photographed as a cut-out with nothing underneath it. There is no surface for it to rest on and nothing for it to cast a shadow onto. No floor, no ground plane, no horizon line, no cast shadow, no contact shadow, no reflection, no vignette, no gradient.

Lighting: flat even studio illumination from all sides, soft and shadowless, like a lightbox. No strong key light, no rim light, no coloured light, no specular blowout, no dramatic highlights. Colours must read as true albedo.

One object only, nothing else in frame. No people, no hands, no other props, no packaging, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows, no borders, no drop shadow.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, clean and undamaged geometry, realistic materials and surface wear. Not stylised, not cartoon, not low-poly, not a 3D render preview, not a wireframe.

license.notice: Fully synthetic. No third-party scanned or scraped geometry.

review.critique: FINAL VERDICT. Overall visual fidelity 0.90. 1,120/2,000 triangles, 2/4 draw calls, 1/2 materials, 2/4 unique geometries, one 256 px canvas at 0.25 MB. Open frame: turntable run with --allow-holes (the bays between rungs are real open bays, not tears).

The plate is a two-rung stand-in (proxy w/h 0.614): the residual is the declared aspect, arithmetic in the spec.

Galvanised 100 x 220 mm plates at x +-0.29 on the wall plane with three bolt heads each, outboard of the stiles as the plate shows; plate #d0d4d2 off region-plate (0.86), bolts #c4c6c8, nuts #b08a3c, rust sleeves #8c5228; rust-bloom tile sparse over clean paint.

name: Fire Escape Ladder Segment
nameTh: บันไดหนีไฟแบบต่อ
notes: A plain uncaged steel escape ladder bolted flat up the back or side wall of Bangkok shophouses, apartment blocks and small office buildings: two flat-bar stiles, round rungs, standoff brackets, and NO safety cage -- no hoops, no vertical cage bars. It is a repeating piece: one straight 3.0 m section with no landing, no top exit and no bottom hook, so a level builder stacks N of them up any wall -- five for a 15 m walk-up, seven for a 21 m condominium -- and reaches the parapet of a building of any height. It stacks in 3.0 m steps rather than matching a floor pitch because this ladder has no per-floor landings; the kit's buildings use 2.8, 3.0 and 3.2 m floors and a 3.0 m module reaches within half a floor of any of their parapets, which is where a real one is cut. Joint contract: pivot is back-center on the wall plane at the bottom edge, so the next segment sits at +3.0 m on Y with the same wall alignment; rungs at 0.30 m pitch with the first rung 0.15 m above the bottom edge (ten per segment) so the rung pitch continues across the joint; stiles run the full 3.0 m and are cut flat at both ends with no end plate, so stacked segments read as one continuous ladder. One bracket pair per segment, on the bottom edge only -- the top of a segment is held by the bracket of the one above -- so stacking never doubles a bracket at a joint. Envelope: 0.7 m wide across the outboard bolt plates (stiles 0.45 m apart centre to centre, 45 x 60 mm flat bar, bracket plates 100 mm wide centred at +-0.29 m), 0.26 m deep from the wall plane to the front face of the stiles (stiles stand 0.2 m off the wall on the brackets). Depth reduced from the earlier 0.85 m declaration on 2026-08-28 when the cage was removed: 0.85 was wall-to-outside-of-cage, and with no cage the deepest element is the stile at 0.20 + 0.06 m. Placement wall, not breakable. Top termination and ground-level drop section are NOT included and would be separate assets if a stack should look finished at either end.
